introduction.p: Some optimization problems choose a path rather than a dimension or price. Reflection and refraction can be derived by minimizing travel time within a specified family of paths. We will write the travel time as a function of the crossing or reflection point and use its derivative to find the minimizing path.

exercise.title: Why does a shortest path produce the law of reflection?

statement.p: A reflected ray from A to a mirror to B minimizes total path length. In your own words, why does that optimization problem force equal angles of incidence and reflection, and why do the derivative and the straight-line-to-the-mirror-image geometry say the same thing?

hint.p: The unknown is the strike point on the mirror. Setting the derivative of total length to zero is the calculus version of unfolding the path into a straight line.

subsection.title: Refraction and Snell’s law
subsection.p: Reflection minimizes distance because the light stays in one medium. Refraction is different.
When light passes from one medium into another, its speed changes. The best path is not the shortest path. It is the path of least time.

exercise.title: Why can least time differ from least distance?

statement.p: Reflection stays in one medium, so least distance and least time agree. Refraction changes speed at a boundary. In your own words, why is the best refracted path a least-time path rather than a shortest path, and what does Snell’s law record about that tradeoff?

hint.p: Time is length divided by speed. If the two speeds differ, a detour through the faster medium can be quicker than the geometrically shortest broken line.

subsection.title: The seed of the calculus of variations
subsection.p: In reflection and refraction, the unknown was one number:

p.me: x=\text{the point where the ray hits a line}.

subsection.p: A more general problem varies an entire path.

Imagine a landscape where the speed depends on position. Perhaps the ground is easy to cross in one region and slow in another. A traveler wants to move from A to B in the least time. Which path should the traveler choose?
A straight line may not be best. A path that detours through faster ground might take less time.

A path is no longer described by one variable. It is described by many choices:
or, in the limit, by a whole function.
The quantity being minimized is not an ordinary function of one number. It is a rule that takes a path as input and returns a number as output:

note.title: Extremal principle
note.p: A physical path is often characterized by making some quantity stationary:

p.me: \text{small changes in the path produce no first-order change in the quantity.}

note.p: For light in simple settings, the quantity is travel time.

subsection.p: A stationary path has zero first-order change in travel time under the allowed small path variations. This condition does not by itself establish an absolute minimum.
That is the same idea we used for ordinary critical points. There, a number x was chosen so that
Here, a path is chosen so that the first-order change of a whole accumulated quantity is zero.

This is the beginning of the calculus of variations. We will not develop that subject here. But it points to the next major need. To measure time, work, area, mass, and probability, we need a way to add infinitely many small contributions.
That is the integral.

exercise.title: Why is a path a different kind of unknown from a number?

statement.p: The reflection and refraction examples vary one crossing point. A functional instead takes an entire path as input and returns a number such as time or length. Explain how this changes the optimization problem.

hint.p: A path is described by many small choices, or in the limit by a whole function. The usual derivative with respect to one number is no longer enough.
